headline: Late bloomers
body: 19 treated boys. 21 untreated controls. Followed to final height.
punch: The result is still the most useful thing on this topic.

headline: Constitutional delay
body: Growth and puberty arrive late, bone age lags chronological age, and adult height usually lands in the normal range anyway. The runway is longer, not shorter.
punch: Which raises an obvious question about treating it.

headline: The 1973 study
body: Methyltestosterone, fluoxymesterone or testosterone enanthate. Low doses, averaging about five and a half months of treatment.
punch: Short course, low dose, and a real control group.

headline: The comparison group
body: 21 boys with the same condition, untreated, followed to final height. That control arm is what makes a small 1973 study still worth citing.
punch: Most of what's discussed in this space has no control arm at all.

headline: The thing to understand
body: Androgens accelerate growth velocity and skeletal maturation together. You grow faster now and you close sooner — the two effects arrive as a package.
punch: Feeling like it's working and ending up taller are different outcomes.

headline: Which is why dose
body: Low dose and short duration is the entire design logic: enough to start puberty moving, not enough to burn the remaining bone age.
punch: The restraint is the treatment. Not the androgen.

headline: And why more
body: Higher doses over longer periods push skeletal maturation faster than they push growth. That's the mechanism by which treatment intended to add height subtracts it.
punch: The failure mode of this drug class is doing more of it.

headline: The honest framing
body: Constitutional delay usually resolves into normal adult height on its own. The intervention question is about distress and timing, not about final centimetres.
punch: Waiting is an active choice with real evidence behind it.
